opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think "unapologetic" is the right word, and I'd stand by it. When I started that work, I didn't have a theory that predicted these sparse subnetworks would exist and train well from the start. What I had was a question and a lot of GPUs. The honest thing was to run the experiment carefully, look at what happened, and report it as clearly as I could, even without a satisfying explanation.

I think there's sometimes pressure in machine learning to dress empirical findings up in theory to make them look more respectable, and too often you get a theorem with assumptions that don't match the setting anyone cares about. I'd rather tell you exactly what I observed, under what conditions, and where it broke. It did break. The original procedure didn't scale cleanly to larger networks, and that led to follow-up work on rewinding to an early point in training rather than all the way to initialization. I see that as the empirical approach working, not failing. You make a claim, you push on it, you find its edges.

Deep learning is, in a lot of ways, a natural science right now. We've built these systems, but we don't understand them, so we have to study them the way a biologist studies an organism: careful observation, controlled experiments, and humility about what you can claim. Theory is wonderful when it catches up, and I hope it does. But I don't think empirical work should have to apologize for coming first. Often it's what tells the theorists what's worth explaining.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he lacked a predictive theory and chose careful empirical experiments, but it does not attribute that approach to being unaware of alternative methods or differing opinions about them.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's important to be clear about what that paper is and isn't. It's a science paper, not an engineering paper. We weren't trying to build a faster way to train networks or ship a pruning method you could drop into production. We were trying to understand something about neural networks that didn't make sense to us, which is why you can train a huge, overparameterized network, throw away most of the weights afterward, and the thing still works, yet if you try to train that small network from scratch it falls apart.

So the approach was, let's run the experiment. Let's take the sparse network we found by pruning, rewind it to its original initialization, and see what happens. And it turned out that it trains just fine. That's an empirical observation. We didn't have a theory for why, and I didn't want to pretend we did. I think the field sometimes has a tendency to dress up an empirical finding with a little bit of math that gives it an air of rigor it hasn't earned. I'd rather say plainly: here's what we observed, here are the controls, here are the random reinitialization baselines that show it isn't an artifact of the structure alone, and here's where it stops working, because it does stop working at larger scales without some modifications.

I came out of a systems and security background before I got into machine learning, and that community is very comfortable with the idea that you learn about a complicated artifact by poking at it. Nobody has a closed-form theory of how an operating system behaves under load. You measure it. Neural networks right now feel much more like that than like a branch of mathematics. We have these objects we built but don't understand, and the honest way to study them is to form a hypothesis, design an experiment that could falsify it, and report what you find, including the negative results.

That last part matters a lot to me. The follow-up work, where we showed the original method breaks on ResNet-50 and ImageNet unless you rewind to an early point in training rather than to initialization, was in some ways more important than the original paper, and it's the kind of thing you only find if you're committed to being empirical rather than defending a clean story. So I don't apologize for it at all. I think the lottery ticket hypothesis is a hypothesis in the real scientific sense. It's a claim about the world that invites people to try to break it. Some of them have, in useful ways, and that's exactly how it's supposed to go.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains the empirical approach as a deliberate choice grounded in scientific goals and his systems background. It does not attribute that approach to being unaware of alternative methods or differing opinions.

astra-6.text:
I think it was the right approach for the question we were asking. We had this intuition: maybe, inside a large randomly initialized network, there’s a much smaller network that could train successfully on its own. And the first thing to do was to see whether that actually happened. I didn’t have a theory that told me it should happen, and I didn’t want to pretend that I did.

The important distinction, to me, is between being empirical and being unprincipled. You can do careful experiments, formulate a hypothesis, try to break it, and be precise about where the evidence supports it. That’s a very useful contribution, even if you can’t yet explain the mechanism mathematically.

And there are limits. Finding a small network after training and pruning a large one doesn’t mean you know how to find that small network cheaply beforehand. You have to keep those claims separate. But establishing that the phenomenon exists gives us something concrete to explain. I think that’s a perfectly good place for science to start.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Frankle lacked a theory for the hypothesis and favored testing it empirically, but does not say he was unaware of alternative methods or differing views about them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think unapologetically empirical is a fair description. We had this observation that seemed surprising, and the first thing I wanted to do was figure out whether it was real. Can we repeat it? Under what conditions does it happen? Where does it break down? I didn’t have a theory that told me what the answer ought to be, and I didn’t want that to stop us from asking the question.

To me, that’s a perfectly reasonable way to do science. You observe something, you try to isolate what’s going on, and hopefully that gives you a phenomenon worth explaining. With the lottery ticket hypothesis, the claim was that these networks contain smaller subnetworks that, with the right initialization, can train successfully on their own. That’s something we could test directly.

The danger is getting ahead of the evidence—taking an experiment in one setting and turning it into a universal statement about neural networks. So I’m very comfortable with the empirical approach, provided we’re careful about what we’ve actually demonstrated and honest about what we still don’t understand.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Frankle lacked a theory predicting the result and wanted to test the observation, but does not say he was unaware of other methodological approaches or differing opinions about them.
